topic: Bayes' Theorem and Independence: Unlocking Predictive Logic

sections.title: Prerequisite Review: Conditional Probability
sections.content: Briefly revisit the idea of 'updating' knowledge. Use a Venn diagram showing two overlapping circles (A and B). Define P(A|B) as the proportion of A inside the B space. Focus on how narrowing our focus to B changes the sample space.
sections.example: A deck of cards: If we know a card is 'Red' (Condition), what is the probability it is a 'Heart'? We ignore all black cards entirely.

sections.title: Defining Independence
sections.content: Define independence visually: Two events A and B are independent if P(A|B) = P(A). Graphically show two non-overlapping or independent events where the presence of B does not shift the density of A. Explain that if A and B are independent, they share no 'predictive information'.
sections.example: Flipping a coin (Event A) and rolling a die (Event B). The result of the coin flip does not physically restrict the outcomes of the die.

sections.title: Introduction to Bayes' Theorem
sections.content: Introduce the theorem as a bridge between 'Prior' beliefs and 'Posterior' evidence. Display the formula: P(A|B) = [P(B|A) * P(A)] / P(B). Use an animation where a probability 'tree' branches out, then we 'reverse' the perspective to find the cause of an observed effect.
sections.example: A medical test: We know the accuracy of the test (P(B|A)) and the prevalence of the disease (P(A)). We use Bayes to find the probability of actually having the disease given a positive result.

sections.title: Connecting Bayes and Independence
sections.content: Discuss the 'Independence Case' in Bayes' Theorem. Explain that if B is independent of A, then P(B|A) = P(B), which simplifies the theorem to P(A|B) = P(A). This demonstrates that if evidence provides no new information, our prior remains unchanged.
sections.example: Detecting a 'Smart Robot' (A) based on whether it rains (B). Since rain is independent of the robot's design, observing rain provides zero information about the robot's identity.

sections.title: Practical Application Summary
sections.content: Synthesize the two concepts: Bayes' allows us to quantify learning, while Independence tells us when learning is impossible. Use a visual 'Decision Matrix' to summarize when to apply these logic gates in real-world scenarios.
sections.example: A squirrel searching for hidden nuts (A). If the squirrel hears a rustle (B), Bayes helps update the location. If the rustle is just wind (independent of nuts), the squirrel ignores it.
